And I don't rush straight at him and risk botching the job halfway through. No, I start far off to one side and approach him gradually, so he never imagines I'm about to strike. Then suddenly he's flat on his back, with no idea how it happened. That was my approach to brother Dowley. I began speaking in a relaxed, easygoing way, as though I only wanted to pass the time. The oldest man alive couldn't have plotted my starting point and guessed where I would end up:

“Boys, when you look closely, there are plenty of curious things about law, custom, convention, and all that—and about the direction and progress of human opinion and activity, too. Written laws exist, and they die out; but there are also unwritten laws, and _those_ last forever. Consider the unwritten law of wages: it says they must increase, little by little, throughout the centuries. Now look at how it works. We know what people are paid today in this place, that place, and somewhere else. We take the average and call that today's wage. We also know the wages of a hundred years ago and two hundred years ago. We can't go back any farther, but that's enough to establish the law of progress, the size and rate of the regular increases. So without a single document to guide us, we can work out fairly accurately what wages were three, four, and five hundred years ago. So far, so good. Do we stop there? No. We stop looking into the past, turn around, and apply the same law to the future. My friends, I can tell you what people will earn on any future date you choose, for hundreds upon hundreds of years.”

“What, my good man? What!”

“Yes. Seven hundred years from now, wages here in your district will be six times their present level. Farm workers will receive three cents a day, and skilled workers six.”

“I wish I could die now and live then!” interrupted Smug the wheelwright, his eyes shining with splendid greed.

“And that's not everything. They'll be fed as well—such food as it is; it won't make them fat. Two hundred and fifty years after that—listen carefully—a skilled worker's wages will be—and remember, this is a law, not a guess—his wages will be _twenty_ cents a day!”

Everyone gasped in awed amazement. Dickon the mason lifted his eyes and hands and murmured:

Then I recited inwardly that entire beautiful passage describing Dante's arrival in the earthly Paradise, and imagined how sweet it would be, while roaming those lovely shores, to behold the chariot of radiance descend and restore my long-lost father to me. Waiting there for that expected hour, I fancied how I would gather the fair flowers about me, twine a garland, and crown myself in gladness. I would sing _sul margine d'un rio_, the song my father loved best; my voice, floating through the unmoving air, would tell him, in whatever bower he awaited our reunion, that his daughter had arrived. The imprint of suffering would then have left my brow, and I could lift my gaze without fear to his eyes, which always shone with the tender light of blameless affection. Thinking of the enchantment in those profound eyes, I shed tears, but softly, afraid my sobbing might trouble the fairy vision.

So completely did this reverie possess me that I walked on without regarding my way, until I actually bent to pluck a blossom for my wreath upon that barren plain where no flowers grew. Then I emerged from my waking dream and found myself in a place I could not recognise.

The sun was down, and the rosy colour borrowed by the clouds from his declining light had almost vanished. Wind swept over the plain. I glanced about and could discover nothing to reveal my whereabouts; I was lost, and tried in vain to recover my path. Still I wandered, while the gathering darkness obscured every mark that might have guided me. At last the deepest blackness of night covered everything. Weariness overcame me, and, remembering that my servant intended sleeping that night in the nearby village, so nobody would be troubled by my absence, and that this wilderness offered safety from any intruder, I determined to remain where I was until morning. Indeed, exhaustion prevented further walking. The air was cold, but bodily discomfort mattered little to me; I believed myself thoroughly accustomed to exposure after two solitary years in which the turning seasons had never interrupted my continual roaming.

I stretched myself on the grass amid darkness unpierced by the smallest ray of light. No sound could be heard, for the profound night had sent even the insects to sleep, the sole inhabitants of that lonely place where neither tree nor bush offered shelter to any other creature. A marvellous stillness filled the air, soothing my senses while quickening my spirit; my thoughts sped from vision to vision and seemed to encompass eternity.

“Then we put up a wire fence.”

“A wire fence?”

“Yes. You suggested it yourself two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember—when the Church first tested its strength against us, then decided it would be wiser to wait for a more promising time. Well, how have you set up the fence?”

“Twelve extremely strong wires—bare, without insulation—run from a large dynamo inside the cave. The dynamo has just two brushes, one positive and one negative—”

“Yes, that's right.”

“The wires leave the cave and enclose a circle of flat ground a hundred yards across. They form twelve separate fences, spaced ten feet apart—twelve circles, one inside another—and their ends run back into the cave.”

“Good. Continue.”

“The fences are attached to heavy oak posts, set just three feet apart and buried five feet deep.”

“That sounds solid enough.”

“Yes. There are no ground connections for the wires outside the cave. They run from the dynamo's positive brush, and the negative brush is grounded. The wires' other ends come back inside, and each one has a separate ground connection.”

“No, no, that won't work!”

“Why not?”

“It costs too much—wastes power for nothing. The only ground connection you want is the one through the negative brush. Bring the other end of each wire back into the cave and secure it separately, _without_ grounding it. Now see how economical that is. A cavalry charge comes at the fence. You're using no power and spending no money, because there's only one connection to the ground until the horses hit the wire. As soon as they touch it, they complete the connection to the negative brush _through the earth_ and fall dead. You see? No energy gets used until you need it. Your lightning is waiting, ready like a loaded gun, but it doesn't cost a cent until you fire. Yes, just the one ground connection—”

“Of course! I can't think how I missed that. It's not only cheaper but more effective than the other arrangement. If wires break or become tangled, nothing goes wrong.”

“Exactly, especially if we install an indicator in the cave and disconnect any broken wire. All right, go on. What about the Gatlings?”

“Yes, that's taken care of. At the center of the innermost circle, I've placed thirteen Gatling guns together on a roomy platform six feet high, with plenty of ammunition.”

“Excellent. They cover every approach, and when the Church's knights turn up, there'll be a performance. The top of the cliff above the cave—”
